en.page_title: Case Study: Internal ERP / WMS / MES Platform - Bowei Xu
en.page_description: How I designed and built an internal operations platform (ERP/WMS/MES) as sole developer: a 50+ table schema, order tracking, material traceability, and automated reporting.
en.title: Internal Operations Platform (ERP / WMS / MES)
en.disclaimer: A sanitized write-up of the internal operations system I designed and built as the sole developer at Fuel Cell Store. It covers the order-to-shipment half of the platform; the warehouse and shop-floor half runs on the same database and has its own write-up. Product details and proprietary code are omitted; what follows is architecture and engineering decisions.
en.related: Read the warehouse and materials half of this platform

sections.heading: Context
paragraphs: The company already had an internal system, but it was slow: common lookups and reports took several seconds or worse. It also covered only part of the workflow, so the gaps were filled with spreadsheets and manual entry, and nothing reliably recorded who changed what.
As the sole developer, I designed and built the replacement: more complete, and faster to query. It covers the full order-to-shipment lifecycle on a relational schema of 50+ tables.

The platform has two halves. This one runs order to shipment: orders, builds, shipments, and reporting. The other is warehouse and shop floor: receiving, scan-driven picking, physical counts, and lot-level material traceability. It sits on this same schema and has its own write-up.

sections.heading: Scope
list: Order management: order entry, line items, and a status flow from open to picked to built to shipped
Inventory: finished-goods stock levels, valuation, and manual adjustments, on the same schema the warehouse subsystem writes to
Materials: raw-material procurement, lot-number tracking, consumption logging, and allocation by order
Builds and work orders: production fulfillment tied to order line items
Shipments: carrier and tracking, packing slips, commercial invoices, and customs documents
Reporting and analytics: 40+ reports across orders, inventory, materials, shipping, and sales
Admin: user and role management, bulk imports, audit log, and work-in-progress tracking

sections.heading: Architecture
paragraphs: A monolith, on purpose, in three tiers. PHP renders the UI and holds the business logic, SQL Server is the single source of truth, and attachments sit on the local filesystem.

tiers.label: PHP
tiers.desc: auth, business logic, rendering, cron jobs

architecture.aria: Architecture diagram: the browser talks over HTTP to a single internal Ubuntu Linux server running PHP, SQL Server, and local file storage.

paragraphs_after: Why a monolith rather than microservices? A small internal user base, a one-person team, and no uptime SLA to hit. At that scale, microservices buy operational overhead and little else. I optimized for how fast one person can build and maintain the thing, while staying clear on which parts would have to change first if that stopped being true.

sections.heading: Scale
list: One SQL Server database of 50+ tables covering orders, inventory, builds, and shipments, shared directly by the ERP and the warehouse application; lot-tracked materials live in a separate database on the same server
The audit table is the largest in the schema, past 1,000,000 rows
20 to 30 internal users working in the system at the same time
Any one work order is edited by a single person at a time, enforced by the lock table rather than left to convention
Reports query live operational data and return in under a second

subsections.title: 1. Concurrency control via pessimistic locking
subsections.body: Two operators editing the same work order would silently overwrite each other. Opening a work order now checks the lock table and takes the lock if it is free; saving releases it. A scheduled job clears anything older than five minutes, so an abandoned session cannot sit on a work order indefinitely. The warehouse subsystem reads and writes this same table, so an order locked on the shop floor cannot be checked out here, and the conflict is settled between the two applications rather than inside either one. Pessimistic locking fits because conflicts here are expensive; optimistic version numbers suit a higher-throughput system where they are rare.

subsections.title: 2. Unified audit trail
subsections.body: Every create, update, and delete writes one row to a single audit table: actor, timestamp, object type, object ID, and a readable note. Keeping all modules in one table is what makes "who changed this record" answerable in a single query. The cost is that every operational write drags a synchronous audit write along with it, so the pressure is write concurrency rather than row count. If that becomes the bottleneck, the fix is to move the audit write off the request path, asynchronously or onto its own filegroup. Partitioning would help the archival queries, not the write path.

subsections.title: 3. Real-time reporting without extra infrastructure
subsections.body: Reports query SQL Server directly and draw their charts in the browser from server-emitted JSON. Nothing is precomputed, so nothing is ever stale, and there is no extra infrastructure to run. The cost is that a heavy report competes with live operations; the way out is a read replica for reporting and asynchronous generation for the worst offenders.

subsections.title: 4. Role-based access control
subsections.body: Two roles, admin and normal user, checked at the top of every page against a server-side session. It is simple and fast to reason about, and it cannot express per-record rules. The day it needs to, the path is attribute-based access control, plus a shared session store if this ever runs on more than one server.

subsections.title: 5. Data-integrity discipline
subsections.body: Bad operational data compounds quietly, so the platform catches it at the entry points: duplicate lot-number detection, negative-stock alerts, and reconciliation reports across materials and stock. Queries are parameterized throughout rather than assembled from concatenated strings. In a schema where every table is business-critical, that is not something to leave to discipline.

sections.heading: Results
list: Replaced a slow, incomplete legacy system with one platform covering the full order-to-shipment lifecycle: orders, inventory, materials, builds, and shipments
Designed the schema and query layer so reporting runs against live operational data, with no separate analytics stack to build or keep in sync
Gave the business end-to-end order traceability and an audit trail it had never had
Built, maintained, and extended the platform single-handedly in production

zh.page_title: 案例研究：内部 ERP / WMS / MES 平台 - 徐博伟
zh.page_description: 作为唯一开发者，我如何设计并构建企业内部运营平台（ERP/WMS/MES）：50 多张表的数据库架构、订单跟踪、物料追溯与自动化报表。
zh.title: 企业内部运营平台（ERP / WMS / MES）
zh.disclaimer: 脱敏案例分析。我在 Fuel Cell Store 作为唯一开发者，设计并构建了这套生产环境的内部运营系统。本文覆盖平台中从下单到发货的这一半；仓储与车间那一半跑在同一个数据库上，另有独立案例。产品细节与专有代码已省略，这里只谈架构和工程决策。
zh.related: 查看这套平台的仓储与物料部分

sections.heading: 背景
paragraphs: 公司原本有一套内部系统，但很慢：常用的查询和报表动辄要等上好几秒。它也只覆盖了一部分流程，剩下的缺口靠电子表格和人工录入来补，谁改过什么也没有可靠的记录。
作为唯一开发者，我设计并构建了替代它的平台：覆盖更全，查询更快，基于一套 50+ 张表的关系型库，贯通从下单到发货的完整流程。
平台分两半。本文是从下单到发货的这一半：订单、生产、发货、报表。另一半是仓储与车间：收货、扫码拣货、实物盘点和批次级物料追溯，跑在同一套库上，另有独立案例。

sections.heading: 范围
list: 订单管理：订单录入、明细行，以及从开单到拣货、生产、发货的状态流转
库存：成品库存、估值和人工调整，与仓储子系统写入的是同一套数据表
物料：原材料采购、批号追踪、消耗记录和按订单分配
生产工单：与订单明细行关联的生产履约
发货：承运商与跟踪号、装箱单、商业发票和报关单据
报表与分析：覆盖订单、库存、物料、发货和销售的 40+ 份报表
管理：用户与角色管理、批量导入、审计日志和在制品跟踪

sections.heading: 架构
paragraphs: 刻意做成单体，分三层。PHP 渲染界面并承载业务逻辑，SQL Server 是唯一数据源，附件放在本地文件系统。

architecture.host: 公司内部的单台 Ubuntu Linux 服务器

tiers.label: PHP
tiers.desc: 鉴权、业务逻辑、渲染、定时任务

architecture.aria: 架构图：浏览器通过 HTTP 访问公司内部的单台 Ubuntu Linux 服务器，服务器上运行 PHP、SQL Server 和本地文件存储。

paragraphs_after: 为什么是单体而不是微服务？用户量小、一个人的团队、没有必须守住的可用性 SLA。这个规模下，微服务买来的只有运维负担。我优化的是一个人能多快把它建起来、维护下去，同时心里有数：哪天这个前提不成立了，哪些部分要最先改。

sections.heading: 规模
list: 单个 SQL Server 数据库，50+ 张表，覆盖订单、库存、生产和发货，由 ERP 和仓库应用直接共用；批次物料在同一台服务器上另有独立数据库
审计表是库中最大的一张，超过 100 万行
20 到 30 名内部用户同时在系统中作业
任何一张工单同一时刻只由一个人编辑，这由锁表强制保证，而不是靠约定
报表直接查询线上业务数据，返回时间在 1 秒以内

subsections.title: 1. 以悲观锁实现并发控制
subsections.body: 两个人同时编辑同一张工单，会静默地覆盖掉对方的改动。现在打开工单会先查锁表，空闲就加锁，保存时释放。定时任务清掉任何超过五分钟的锁，被弃置的会话占不住工单。仓储子系统读写的是同一张表，所以车间锁住的工单在这边签不出去，冲突是在两套应用之间解决的，而不是各自为政。这里冲突代价高，所以用悲观锁；基于版本号的乐观锁更适合冲突少、吞吐高的场景。

subsections.title: 2. 统一的审计记录
subsections.body: 每一次新增、更新、删除都往同一张审计表写一行：操作者、时间戳、对象类型、对象 ID，外加一条能读懂的备注。所有模块共用一张表，“这条记录谁动过”才能一句 SQL 查出来。代价是每次业务写入都要捎上一次同步的审计写入，压力来自并发写而不是行数。真成了瓶颈，解法是把审计写入从请求路径上挪走：异步写，或者挪到独立文件组。按月分区帮的是归档查询，不是写入路径。

subsections.title: 3. 无需额外基础设施的实时报表
subsections.body: 报表直接查 SQL Server，图表在前端用服务端输出的 JSON 渲染。没有预计算，所以也不存在过期数据，更没有额外的基础设施要养。代价是重报表会和线上操作抢资源；真要扩，就是报表走只读副本，最重的几张改成异步生成。

subsections.title: 4. 基于角色的访问控制
subsections.body: 两个角色，管理员和普通用户，每个页面顶部对着服务端会话校验。简单、快、好推理，缺点是表达不了逐条记录的权限规则。真需要那天，路径是基于属性的访问控制；如果哪天部署到多台服务器，再加一个共享的会话存储。

subsections.title: 5. 数据完整性纪律
subsections.body: 业务数据的错会悄悄累积，所以平台在入口处就拦下来：批号重复检测、负库存告警，以及覆盖物料与库存的对账报表。所有查询一律参数化，不拼字符串。在一套每张表都关乎业务的库上，这种事不能靠自觉。

sections.heading: 成果
list: 用一套平台取代了原先又慢又不全的老系统，覆盖从下单到发货的完整流程：订单、库存、物料、生产、发货
数据库与查询层的设计让报表直接跑在线上业务数据上，不必另建、也不必同步一套分析栈
给了业务此前从未有过的端到端订单追溯和完整审计记录
由单人在生产环境中独立构建、维护和迭代
